abstract: Combinatorial perturbations are widely used to study genetic interactions and to develop drug combinations, but the number of possible combinations grows quadratically with the number of perturbations, and only a small fraction can be measured in a screen experiment. Despite their growing sophistication, deep-learning and foundation models often fail to outperform a simple additive baseline based on measured single-perturbation responses. This suggests a simpler approach that builds on these measurements and directly learns deviations from additivity at the population level. We therefore developed GAIN, a lightweight model that implements these principles by predicting the pseudobulk response to a combination as the sum of its two single-perturbation responses and a learned interaction term. Across three single-cell datasets of genetic and drug combinations, GAIN corrected deviations from additivity and outperformed the additive model and cell-level methods across generalization settings and metrics, while training 3- to 64-fold faster. Applied to a combinatorial CRISPR screen of leukemia differentiation regulators, GAIN revealed synergy between key regulators of the differentiation block and genes that restrain differentiation but have little effect alone. It also revealed dampening by the histone chaperone FACT, which supports the induction of differentiation genes. These results establish population-level modeling of the deviation from additivity as a simple, accurate and scalable approach to predicting combination responses.
